Sockets: listening, connecting, and moving bytes.

Three files and one module -- `socket_linux.kh`, `socket_macos.kh` and
`socket_windows.kh` -- of which exactly one is ever in a build;
`khora_db::selected_for_target` is the rule and the file's name is where it
is written. The API below is the same on all three, and the sections at the
end of this page are what differs underneath it.

**No struct crosses the boundary.** `bind` wants a `sockaddr_in`, which is
sixteen bytes; those sixteen bytes are laid out in Khora, in an `Array<U8>`,
and lent as a `Ptr` for exactly the duration of the call. That is what
`docs/design/ffi.md` says a pointer is for, and it is why binding a socket
needs nothing added to the runtime.

## On Linux

Nothing to start up, the handle is a small `int` rather than a pointer-sized
one, and the call that closes it is `close`.

## On macOS

Two differences from Linux, both of them BSD's rather than Apple's: a
`sockaddr_in` begins with a length byte where the Linux one puts the low half
of the family, and the socket-option numbers are the BSD ones. Everything
else -- the calls, the sizes, the byte order -- is the same, which is why this
file is otherwise a copy of `socket_linux.kh`.

**A copy, and that is the mechanism working as designed.** A file suffix
selects a whole file, so a target that differs in two lines still needs a
file of its own. `_posix` exists for the case where Linux and macOS agree
completely, and sockets are not that case. The cost is that a fix to one of
these usually belongs in both.

## On Windows

The Berkeley names with Winsock's differences: `WSAStartup` before anything
else -- which is what `start` is for, and why it is not a no-op here --
`closesocket` rather than `close`, and a `SOCKET` that is a pointer-sized
handle rather than a small `int`.

## Functions

### invalid_handle

```khora
export fn invalid_handle() -> Int
```

A failed call returns -1, and a handle is never negative.

### start

```khora
export fn start() -> Bool
```

Nothing to start. Present so that a caller reads the same on both targets.

### listen_on

```khora
export fn listen_on(port: Int) -> Int
```

A socket listening on `port`, or [`invalid_handle`].

### accept_on

```khora
export fn accept_on(server: Int) -> Int
```

Waits for a connection. [`invalid_handle`] if the wait failed.

### set_receive_timeout

```khora
export fn set_receive_timeout(handle: Int, millis: Int) -> Bool
```

How long a read will wait before giving up, in milliseconds.

See the note on the Windows one for why a server cannot do without it.

**No longer `SO_RCVTIMEO`, and it could not be.** The kernel's option
applies to a call that would have blocked, and a socket the reactor drives
never has one — so it goes silently inert the moment the socket is
prepared, and the slow client it exists to shed would park a fiber for
ever. The runtime keeps the deadline and a scheduler timer enforces it. A
read that runs out still comes back negative, which is what every caller
here already treats as a connection to give up on.

### receive

```khora
export fn receive(connection: Int, buffer: Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Reads what has arrived into `buffer`, and says how many bytes that was.

Zero means the other end closed; negative means the read failed.

### transmit

```khora
export fn transmit(connection: Int, text: String) -> Int
```

Writes `text`, and says how many bytes went. Negative if the write failed.

### connect_to

```khora
export fn connect_to(host: String, port: Int) -> Int
```

Opens a connection to `host` on `port`, or [`invalid_handle`].

**The first thing here that starts a conversation.** Everything else in this
module grew from serving: `listen_on`, `accept_on`, and nothing that dials.
A database driver is the first caller that needs the other direction.

`host` may be a name or an address; resolution, address family and the
platform's own resolver are the runtime's, which is why this is one extern
rather than `getaddrinfo` and two `sockaddr` layouts written three times.
`docs/design/ffi.md` is the boundary and `khora_net_connect` is on the far
side of it.

**It blocks the fiber's worker while it connects.** A DNS lookup is not
something the reactor can wait on. That is once per connection against many
queries, which is the right thing to get wrong first, and it is written
down in `docs/roadmap.md` Phase 13 rather than left to be found.

### transmit_bytes

```khora
export fn transmit_bytes(connection: Int, bytes: Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Writes bytes, and says how many went. Negative if the write failed.

[`transmit`] takes a `String`, which is right for a protocol made of text
and wrong for one made of bytes: a wire protocol frames its messages with a
length nobody wrote as characters. Postgres is the first caller, and a
`String` would have meant deciding what its bytes mean on the way through.

### shut

```khora
export fn shut(handle: Int) ->()
```

Closes a connection, letting the other end finish first.

The same reasoning as the Windows file, and the same shape: closing while
the peer is still writing sends an RST, which discards the answer the peer
had not read yet. `SHUT_WR` is 1 here too.
